passage:
For months Francis had carried the year he left college and told his parents it was a transfer. He wanted Yogesh to know, and he was afraid Yogesh would see him differently. So he began small, on a walk. "I wasn't very good at the job I had at twenty. I quit before they could fire me." Yogesh only nodded and said, "That sounds like a hard time." Nothing changed in his face, and Francis felt his shoulders drop a little.

Three weeks later, on the balcony, he took a breath. "There's something else. I never transferred. I dropped out, and I've been ashamed of it since." His voice shook on the last word.

Yogesh felt honoured and completely unsure what to say. His mind offered him solutions, a phone call to the college, a plan, and he set them all aside. He put a hand on the railing next to Francis's and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you did." He did not ask why. He did not fix it.

Next week Gurpreet asked casually over tea, "What's up with Francis lately? He seems lighter." Yogesh smiled and stirred his cup. "He's doing better. That's all I'll say."

qa.q: What did Francis tell his parents about leaving college?
qa.a: He told them it was a transfer.

qa.q: How did Francis's small first disclosure and Yogesh's quiet reactions connect to the bigger conversation on the balcony?
qa.a: Francis began small on a walk and saw Yogesh nod kindly, so on the balcony he told him he had dropped out. Yogesh said thank you, did not fix it, and told Gurpreet only that Francis was doing better.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when Francis said he had dropped out?
qa.a: He felt honoured and unsure what to say, so he set aside his urge to offer solutions.

qa.q: What could Francis do if he wants to share another old shame with Yogesh later?
qa.a: He could share it at his own pace, a little at a time, and keep noticing whether Yogesh holds it with care.

grounding: A partner's slow confession of an old shame is seen from the person who fears judgment and the person who listens and keeps the confidence.

passage:
Jasleen skipped the second meeting, and the third. The presentation was three weeks away and she told herself that Nandini and Sabina would sort it. They always did. She scrolled through videos while the shared document stayed half empty.

Nandini opened the same document at eleven that night and did another set of slides. She was tired, and she could feel resentment growing like a stone in her shoe. Sabina sent a note: "I'm on my third section too." Nandini almost kept doing it in silence. Then she didn't. She wrote in the chat, "Can we set who does what? I'll do the data. Sabina has the intro. Jasleen, can you take the conclusion and send it by Thursday? Let's check in Tuesday."

Jasleen read it and felt her cheeks go warm. She saw that it had been unfair, that two people had been holding her weight. She wrote her section that night, and it was not perfect, but it was hers. At the presentation Nandini went first, Sabina second. Jasleen, when it was her turn, said, "I did the conclusion, and Nandini and Sabina did most of the rest."

qa.q: Whose turn was it to write the conclusion?
qa.a: Jasleen was asked to take the conclusion.

qa.q: How did the slide work look from Jasleen's side and from Nandini's side, and what changed after the chat message?
qa.a: Jasleen skipped meetings and told herself Nandini and Sabina would sort it, while Nandini did slides at night and felt resentment. After Nandini wrote who does what and asked for the conclusion by Thursday, Jasleen wrote her own section.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling as she opened the shared document at eleven at night?
qa.a: She felt tired and resentful, like a stone in her shoe.

qa.q: What could Nandini do next time a group project starts this way?
qa.a: She could set roles at the start, check in early, and raise it politely well before the deadline instead of doing everything silently.

grounding: A group project is seen from the member who lets others cover and the member who carries the load until she speaks up.

passage:
In the review meeting Pradeep took the client account from Urmila and gave it to a newer favourite. Urmila said, "That doesn't match the numbers." Pradeep smiled thinly. "If you keep pushing, your renewal might get looked at again." A couple of people looked at their laptops. Urmila's cheeks burned, and she said nothing more in the room.

Leela watched from the corner and knew it was unfair. Her stomach hurt. She needed her job, the rent was due, and speaking up could put her next. She thought about it honestly for a night: what could go wrong, what silence would cost. She found Urmila at the pantry and said, "I saw what happened. Can I help?"

Urmila had already started noting dates and the exact words in a notebook. "I'm taking it to HR, and to Ms. Iyer, the senior director." She felt shaky, but she wasn't going to accept it as normal. Leela took a breath and wrote a calm email that stuck to what she had witnessed, and sent it to HR too.

Two days later Ms. Iyer asked both of them to come to her office. Leela's hands were cold, and she went anyway.

qa.q: Who was the senior director Urmila planned to approach?
qa.a: Ms. Iyer.

qa.q: How did Urmila's and Leela's views of the meeting differ, and what did each do afterwards?
qa.a: Urmila was the one threatened, so she kept dated notes and took it to HR and a senior director. Leela was afraid for her own job but weighed the risk, offered help and sent a calm written account of what she had seen.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling in the corner of the review meeting?
qa.a: She felt afraid and uneasy, since she knew it was unfair but needed her job.

qa.q: What could Urmila do if Pradeep keeps threatening her after the HR meeting?
qa.a: She could keep her records up to date, ask the senior director for support, and look at her options.

grounding: A manager's unfair decision is seen from the colleague who is threatened for disagreeing and the witness who is afraid to speak.

passage:
Omkar had built a tall block fort and he wanted to be the boss of it. When Minakshi came over with a flag, he put his hand up. "No girls!" A boy beside him copied him, "No girls," and then it sounded like a rule. Omkar felt big and important, and didn't think about how it landed.

Minakshi stopped. A heavy stone dropped into her tummy and her eyes prickled. She walked away and stood near the shelf, blinking hard. She thought about crying, then she went to Rukmini, the teacher, and said, "They said I can't play."

Rukmini took her hand and went over to the fort. She crouched to Omkar's level. "Omkar, if someone said 'no you' to you, how would that feel?" Omkar was quiet. "Bad," he said. "Like a stone." The teacher waited. Then he looked at Minakshi and said, in a small voice, "Come and play." Minakshi held up the flag. "Where does it go?" The other boy shuffled aside and made a gap in the wall, and the flag went on top.

qa.q: What did Minakshi bring to the block fort?
qa.a: She brought a flag.

qa.q: How did the words no girls feel to Omkar and to Minakshi, and what did Rukmini change?
qa.a: Omkar felt big and important and did not think about the hurt, while Minakshi felt a stone in her tummy. Rukmini helped Omkar remember how it feels to be told no, and he said come and play.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling as she stood near the shelf blinking hard?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sad, like a stone in her tummy, and close to crying.

qa.q: How could the teacher help if the boys try to make no girls a group rule again?
qa.a: The teacher could help the children imagine how it feels to be left out, and show them how to say come and play, so it does not become a rule.

grounding: A child's exclusion in a block-fort game is seen from the one who says no to feel powerful and the one who is turned away.

passage:
Chaitanya had been driving the red fire truck around the mat for ten minutes when Irfan took it from behind. Chaitanya's face went hot and his fists curled tight. "MINE!" he shouted, and he yanked at the truck, nearly hitting Irfan's arm.

Irfan felt small and scared. His arm stung where the truck knocked it. His own fist tightened, because hitting back seemed like the fastest thing, but he opened it again. He took a step back and said in a wobbly voice, "Stop, that hurts." Then he ran to Samir, the teacher, who was helping with paint.

Samir came over, calm and without hurry. He crouched by Chaitanya. "I can see your fists. You are very angry. Can you tell me in words?" Chaitanya's chest was going up and down. "I am angry. I want it back." "Good. Let's take three big breaths first." They breathed together, one, two, three. Then Samir turned to Irfan. "Irfan, you took it without asking, and it scared him. And Chaitanya, you hurt Irfan's arm by pulling." Samir set the truck in the middle. "You each get a turn. I'll count."

qa.q: What colour was the truck the boys fought over?
qa.a: The fire truck was red.

qa.q: How did the grabbing feel to Chaitanya and to Irfan, and what did Samir do for each?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt hot and furious and shouted mine, while Irfan felt small and scared and said stop, that hurts. Samir helped Chaitanya say he was angry in words and breathe, and he heard Irfan's side and set turns.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he closed his tightened fist again?
qa.a: He felt scared and small, and he wanted to hit back but chose not to.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya try next time someone takes his toy?
qa.a: He could say I am angry, I want it back, take a breath, and ask a teacher for help instead of snatching.

grounding: A toy grab is seen from the child who flares up and the child who feels scared, with a teacher helping both.

passage:
Chandrika scrolled through Ankita's photos each night: the beach trip, the matching jackets, the friends who tagged her in everything. It stung. She typed a comment under a picture, then read it back. It was half a joke and mostly mean. She deleted it. A memory came to her instead, of Ankita hiding in the library the week before the school play, gripping her script. Perhaps every picture hid a week like that. Chandrika put the phone down and signed up for the debate club, which she'd been avoiding.

Ankita noticed that people said things like, "You're so lucky, everything works out for you," and smiled while they said it, but the smile did not reach the eyes. She kept her tone kind. "Thanks, I got nervous a lot too." She knew not every compliment was friendship. She kept Nazia close, who sat beside her at lunch and never asked about the photos.

On Friday, after debate club, Chandrika said, "You were great in the play." Ankita looked at her for a second. "Honestly, I was terrified. Thank you for saying it." Chandrika laughed. "I couldn't tell."

qa.q: What club did Chandrika sign up for?
qa.a: She signed up for the debate club.

qa.q: How did Chandrika's envy and Ankita's sense of it fit together?
qa.a: Chandrika studied Ankita's photos and felt envy, nearly writing a mean comment, while Ankita felt the envy behind compliments like everything works out for you. Chandrika turned toward her own strengths and Ankita stayed kind and honest, keeping Nazia close.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling as she read back the comment she had typed?
qa.a: She felt envious and stung, and uneasy that her joke was mostly mean.

qa.q: What could Ankita do if a classmate's compliments keep sounding like envy?
qa.a: She could stay kind and honest without assuming all the attention is friendship, and keep her few real friends like Nazia close.

grounding: Envy of a popular classmate is seen from the student who studies her life online and the popular student who senses envy in the compliments.
